fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces: Exercises

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Worked homework for Three Easy Pieces, one chapter per chapter of the book. The conceptual material lives in the concept pages — Process, Process API, Process control block for the process abstraction; fork(), wait(), exec(), Unix signals for the process API; FIFO scheduling, SJF scheduling, Round-robin scheduling for the schedulers. Simulator questions are answered twice over: what I predicted before running anything, then what the tool actually printed. The prediction is the experiment, and the ones I got wrong are the entries worth rereading.

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Completion time when one process blocks on I/O

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: IO_RUN_LATER wastes the overlap it just bought

fr:mainmatter.html:p: With -I IO_RUN_LATER, a completed I/O does not immediately return the issuing process to the CPU; whatever was running keeps running. fr:title.text: fork() copies the address space, not the variable

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: fork() copies the address space, not the variable

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Write a program that calls fork(). Before forking, set a variable — say x — to 100. What is its value in the child? What happens when parent and child both change it?

html:span.style: font-family: var(--sans); font-size: 11pt; font-weight: 500; color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.65);

Multiplying X (B \times D) and Y (D \times F) in int8.

html:ol.html:li: How many bytes loaded from memory?
How many total OPs performed?
What is arithmetic intensity?
What is roofline estimate for T_{math} and T_{comms}? What are reasonable upper and lower bounds for runtime of whole operation?

html:span.style: font-family: var(--sans); font-size: 11pt; font-weight: 500; color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.65);

html:ol.html:li: The only difference here from before is that the loaded / written bytes are divided by 2. This means we load BD bytes for X and DF bytes for Y, which is a total of BD + DF bytes.
The same number of total ops is performed. Namely, for each element in the output matrix (BF of them) we must perform 2D OPs. This leaves a total of 2DBF OPs.
The arithmetic intensity is now just 2 \times the old arithmetic intensity because we are loading half as many bytes i.e. \frac {2DBF}{BD + DF + BF}.
html:ol.html:div:
Remark. After looking at the solution, they also mention that the rule on batch size to saturate arithmetic intensity remains unchanged. Namely, using the heuristic B \ll D, F, we can get that the arithmetic intensity \approx \frac {2DBF}{DF} = 2B. One may think that this means that we can use smaller batch size. However, recall that our in8 peak OPs/s has now doubled to 3.94e14. Therefore, the computation is effectively 2B > \frac {2 \cdot \text {Peak OPs / s}}{\text {HBM Bandwidth}} \iff B > \frac {\text {Peak OPs / s}}{\text {HBM Bandwidth}} = 240
Question. So what is the point of int8?
Answer.Within each batch, we are actually performing FLOPs 2 \times as fast. Therefore, our computation is actually twice as fast wall clock time!
html:ol.html:li: From above, we know that we are performing 2DBF FLOPs. Assuming our int8 peak OPs/s is 3.94e14, this gives T_{math} = \frac {2DBF}{3.94e14}. Similarly, we have that T_{comm} = \frac {BD + DF + BF}{8.2e11}. We know that \max \{T_{max}, T_{comm}\} is a good lower bound, and that T_{max} + T_{comm} is a good upper bound.

fr:tree.fr:mainmatter:
Say you want to sample from a 200B parameter model in bf16 that’s split across 32 TPU v4p. How long would it take to load all the parameters from HBM into the systolic array? Hint: use the numbers above.
Solution
I am a bit stumped to start. However, since we only care about loading the parameters, the relevant number is HBM BW (1.2e12). Since there is no communication between chips yet (I think). ICI bandwidth is not yet relevant? Since each chip has its own HBM, the effective bandwidth should be 32 \cdot 1.2e12 = 3.84e13. Therefore, we should have (2e11 \cdot 16) / 3.84e13 = 0.0833\text {s}
Remark. After looking at solution, this turned out right?

Consider a full TPU v5e pod. How many total CPU hosts are there? How many TPU TensorCores? What is the total FLOPs/s for the whole pod? What is the total HBM? Do the same exercise for TPU v5p pod.
Solution
TPU v5e. From the TPU specs, a TPU v5e has a pod size of 16\times 16 and a host size of 4\times 2. Therefore, I believe this means that there are 8 CPU hosts. The v5e is an inference chip, so it only has one tensor core per chip. Across 16\times 16 chips this gives 256 tensor cores. Similarly, from the TPU specs I think we can just multiply the FLOPS/s per chip and HBM per chip to get 256\cdot 1.97e14 bf16 FLOPs/s and 256\cdot 8.2e11 bytes/s.
TPU v5p. The only distinction here besides swapping the numbers is that each chip has two tensor cores. Combining this with the larger pod size, we get 2\cdot 16\cdot 20\cdot 28 tensor cores per pod.
Remark. After looking at solution, it seems I misunderstood what host size meant. The host size is the topology of the subunit connected to a single host. So the number of hosts is actually the pod size / host size. This gives (16\cdot 16) / (4\cdot 2) for the v5e and (16\cdot 20\cdot 28) / (2\cdot 2\cdot 1) for the v5p.

Imagine we’re forced to store a big weight matrix A of type bf16[D,F], and a batch of activations x of type bf16[B,D] in host DRAM and want to do a matrix multiplication on them. This is running on a single host, and we’re using a single TPU v6e chip attached to it. You can assume B≪DB≪D , and F=4DF=4D.
Solution
I assume this is streaming directly from PCIe without any tiling in VMEM / HBM? Relevant number TPU v6e can do 9.2e14 FLOPs/s. From previous chapter, we know that for bf16 matmul we need B = \text {intensity}(\text {computation}) \geq \text {intensity}(\text {accelerator}) = (\text {FLOPs/s}) / (\text {bytes/s})
Therefore, we need B \geq \frac {9.2e14}{1.6e10}
This is a very large batch size compared to HBM we saw in the previous chapter.

Let’s say we want to multiply a weight matrix int8[16384, 4096] by an activation matrix of size int8[B, 4096] where B is some unknown batch size. Let’s say we’re on 1 TPU v5e to start.
How long will this multiplication take as a function of B?
What if we wanted to run this operation out of VMEM? How long would it take as a function of B?
Solution
For the first part, we need to load 16384 \cdot 4096 + 4096B~\text {bytes}
and store B \cdot 16384 bytes. We need to perform 2\cdot B\cdot 16384\cdot 4096~\text {FLOPs}
Therefore, the communication time is T_{comm} = (16384 \cdot 4096 + 4096\cdot B + 16384\cdot B)/8.2e11
and the math time is T_{math} = (2\cdot B\cdot 16384\cdot 4096)/3.94e14
The total computation time will then be \max \{T_{math}, T_{comm}\} and the ridge point is when T_{math} = T_{comm}. This gives us
\begin {align*} \frac {2\cdot B\cdot 16384\cdot 4096}{3.94e14} &= \frac {16384 \cdot 4096 + 4096\cdot B + 16384\cdot B}{8.2e11} \\ &\iff B = 259 \end {align*}
For the second part, VMEM is 10\times faster than HBM. Therefore, our batch size can be 10\times smaller.
Remark. The solution says that VMEM is 22\times faster. So the numbers are adjusted accordingly.

Let’s say we have a TPU v5e 4x4 slice. Let’s say we want to send an array of type bf16[8, 128, 8192] from TPU{0,0} to TPU{3, 3}. Let’s say the per-hop latency for TPU v5e is 1μs.
How soon will the first byte arrive at its destination?
How long will total transfer take?
Solution
I believe since we have wrap-around links in the Torus topology we can make it from (0,0) \to (3,3) in 4 hops. If each hop latency is 1\mu s then it should take 4 \mu s.
From TPU specs, the TPU v5e has ICI bandwidth 4.5e 10. We need to transfer 2\cdot 8\cdot 128\cdot 8192 bytes. Naively, I am going to say that this means it will take \frac {2\cdot 8\cdot 128\cdot 8192}{4.5e 10} s, factoring in latency this gives 372 + 4 \mu s.
Remark. So the wraparound links are actually only on pods of 16 \times 16 or larger. This means it is actually 6 hops from (0,0) \to (3,3). Also, we can use the bi-directional capabilities of the network to half the time it will take to send the whole array.

Imagine you have a big matrix A: int8[128 * 1024, 128 * 1024] sharded evenly across a TPU v5e 4x4 slice but offloaded to host DRAM on each chip. Let’s say you want to copy the entire array to TPU{0, 0} and multiply it by a vector bf16[8, 128 * 1024]. How long will this take?
Solution
From the question wording, we are assuming the vector is already on TPU{0,0}.
From TPU specs, the host configuration for TPU v5e is 4 \times 2. I believe this means in a 4 \times 4 pod there will be 2 CPUs. If this is the case, then for the half of chips on the other host, we first have to transfer to our host via DCN which has bandwidth 3.125e 9 for v5e. Since it is sharded evenly, this would be (1/2) \cdot 128 \cdot 128 \cdot 1024 \cdot 1024 bytes we must send over DCN, taking \frac {(1/2) \cdot 128 \cdot 128 \cdot 1024 \cdot 1024}{3.125e 9} = 2.75 s
However, now looking at the notes again, we only use DCN for chips not connected via ICI (which makes sense because it clearly slow AF).
Instead, we can first transfer all the bytes to the respective chips over PCIe and then to TPU{0,0} over ICI. To load into HBM, PCIe bandwidth is 1.6e 10 bytes/second. Since we can divide across all 16 chips, it will take \frac {128 \cdot 128 \cdot 1024 \cdot 1024}{16\cdot 1.6e 10} = 67.1ms
Now to actually get all of the weights onto a single chip, we can follow the previous part. Using bi-directional bandwidth 9e 10, we have \frac {128 \cdot 128 \cdot 1024 \cdot 1024}{9e 10} = 190.9ms The remaining time comes from \max \{T_{comm}, T_{math}\}, which are T_{math} = \frac {2\cdot 128\cdot 1024\cdot 128 \cdot 1024\cdot 8}{1.97e 14} = 1.39ms and T_{comm} = \frac {128\cdot 1024\cdot 128\cdot 1024 + 2\cdot 8\cdot 128\cdot 1024 + 2\cdot 128\cdot 1024\cdot 8}{8.2e 11} = 20.9ms
Thus, the total is 67.1 + 190.9 + 20.9 = 278.9ms.
Remark.
I think I might be so fucking him it is actually unbelievable. My numbers are all off, but the process seems pretty much the same. I also SNIPED the DCN stuff.
However, it seems there is a bit more nuance to the ICI links than I thought. In particular, our number is a lower bound dependent on the amount of utilized inbound links. Since (0,0) is a corner, it only has 2 links and that is why the denominator is 2\cdot 4.5e 10 and is not because of bi-directional bandwidth. I imagine if there were wraparound links then we could divide the ICI time by 2 because there are 4 total inbound links.

Shard \text {In}[B_{XY}, D], W_{in}[D,F_{XY}]

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Why the MXU pads everything to 128

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What is the native op of one Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU), and why does that force padding to 128?

html:div.html:details:
Answer One bf16[8,128] @ bf16[128,128] -> f32[8,128] every 8 cycles, on a 128 \times 128 systolic array — 256 \times 256 on v6e/Trillium.
The array's side length is fixed in hardware, so any matrix axis shorter than 128 (256 on v6e) is padded up to it, and the FLOPs spent on the padding are simply wasted. With 2–4 MXUs per core, tiling dimensions want to exceed 128 \times the MXU count.
Scale: roughly 5e13 bf16 FLOPs/s per MXU at 1.5 GHz, so about 2e14 per v5e chip. int8 runs ~2\times faster, int4 ~4\times .

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A grid of processing elements in which every operand moves by one hop per cycle to a fixed neighbour, and nothing is addressed. A PE multiplies what arrives at it, adds what arrived from above, and passes the result on. There is no register file to name, no arbitration, and no scheduler: the dataflow is the wiring, and the only freedom in the design is which of the three operands you decide to hold still.

Hold the output still and each PE owns one entry of the result, accumulating in place while both inputs stream past. Hold the weights still — the choice the Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU) makes — and each PE pins one w_{ij} for the whole tile while activations stream in from the left and partial sums fall downward. The second is the one worth being able to draw from memory, because the staggering it requires is where every systolic-array bubble comes from:

The stagger is the whole trick. Row i of the activation tape is held back i cycles, so that x_k arrives at PE(k, j) on precisely the cycle the running sum for column j reaches that row. The set of PEs firing on cycle t is therefore the anti-diagonal i + j = t, and a finished dot product falls out of the bottom of column j having been accumulated on the way down — never written to memory, never read back.
What you pay for that is the fill and the drain. An N \times N array streaming M samples is busy for M + 2N - 2 cycles but does only M N^2 useful multiply-accumulates, so utilisation is

For the four-by-four array above, four samples give 40%. On a real 128 \times 128 MXU the fill is 2N - 2 = 254 cycles, so one isolated 8 \times 128 tile — the shape of the native op — would run at 8/262, near three per cent. That number is not what the hardware achieves, and the gap is the point: consecutive tiles stream in back-to-back with no bubble between them, so the fill is paid once per run of matmuls rather than once per tile. This is the fill bubble, and it is why the cost of a small matmul is dominated by a fixed charge that a large one amortises away.

An sm_XX target is the compute capability a GPU kernel is compiled against — nvcc -arch=sm_90a — and it names an instruction surface, not a performance tier. What follows is the coverage a tensor-core kernel actually has to care about: which MMA instruction family exists, and which of the asynchronous data-movement features it depends on came with it.

html:tr.html:td: mma.sync, ldmatrix, cp.async; no TMA, clusters, or TMEM
mma.sync, ldmatrix, cp.async; FP8 tensor cores, no TMA or TMEM
wgmma + mma.sync; TMA, thread-block clusters, async barriers, DSM

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Read down the third column and the datacenter line tells one story: each generation moves the matrix multiply further away from the individual thread. mma.sync is issued by a warp and the operands live in its registers; wgmma is issued by a warpgroup of four and can read the A operand straight out of shared memory; tcgen05.mma is issued by a single thread on behalf of a CTA pair and keeps its accumulator in Tensor Memory (TMEM), a memory the register file does not see. The data movement follows the same arc — cp.async is a per-thread copy, Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA) is a descriptor a single thread hands to a hardware engine.

The trap in the table is sm_120a. Consumer Blackwell shares the marketing generation with B200 but not the tensor-core path: it has Hopper-era conveniences (TMA, clusters, Distributed Shared Memory (GPU)) and Ampere-era MMA, with no tcgen05 and no TMEM at all. A kernel written against sm_100a does not merely run slower on a 5090 — it does not compile. Treat sm_120a as the branch point in a kernel's dispatch, not as a small delta from sm_100a.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. The trailing a means architecture-specific: the target enables instructions exclusive to that exact chip and gives up forward compatibility, so the resulting cubin will not PTX-JIT onto a later architecture the way a plain sm_90 binary would. Every generation from Hopper on ships its tensor-core ISA only behind an a target, which is why a real build matrix has one entry per row above rather than one per generation. sm_121a is the extreme case — the same instruction surface as sm_120a and still its own cubin.

fr:title.text: The batch size is the intensity

fr:mainmatter.html:p: For a bf16 matmul [B, D] \times [D, F] \to [B, F], give the FLOPs, bytes, intensity, and the resulting rule of thumb.

html:div.html:details:
Answer \text {FLOPs} = 2BDF and \text {bytes} = 2BD + 2DF + 2BF — both operands loaded, the output written, two bytes apiece — so
\mathrm {Intensity} = \frac {BDF}{BD + DF + BF}
With B \ll D, F the DF term dominates the denominator and the intensity collapses to BDF / DF = B. The whole rule of thumb is that the batch size is the intensity: a matmul is compute-bound once the per-replica batch exceeds 240 tokens on TPU (\approx 295 on H100, from 9.89 \times 10^{14} / 3.35 \times 10^{12}).
Three caveats. B counts tokens, not sequences. The threshold is per replica — sharding scales FLOPs and bandwidth together, so it applies to each copy of the weights (Data parallelism). And tiling changes the byte count once the matmul is large enough that the operands no longer fit.

Answer For \mathrm {bf16}[N] \times \mathrm {bf16}[N] \to \mathrm {bf16}[1] the work is N multiplies and N - 1 adds while the traffic is 2N + 2N + 2 bytes, so
\mathrm {Intensity} = \frac {2N - 1}{4N + 2} \longrightarrow \frac {1}{2}
The point is that the intensity is constant in N: there is no size you can grow into to escape it, unlike a matmul whose intensity rises with the batch. Half a FLOP per byte sits far below any ridge point — even the TPU v5p VPU, at roughly 7 \times 10^{12} FLOPs/s per core, wants an intensity near 3.
Reuse is what buys intensity. Every byte loaded into a matmul feeds many FLOPs; in a dot product it feeds one.

fr:title.text: Weight-only int8 halves the compute-bound batch

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Weight-only int8 halves the compute-bound batch

fr:mainmatter.html:p: With weights in int8 but activations and compute in bf16, at what batch size does a matmul become compute-bound?

html:div.html:details:
Answer For \mathrm {bf16}[B, D] \times \mathrm {int8}[D, F] \to \mathrm {bf16}[B, F] the FLOPs are unchanged at 2BDF and still run at the bf16 rate of 1.97 \times 10^{14}, but the weights now cost DF bytes instead of 2DF. With B small the intensity therefore roughly doubles to 2B, and
2B > 240 \implies B > 120
Half the usual threshold — weight-only int8 quantization is an easy win even on hardware you are not using in int8.
Contrast full int8, weights and OPs: the intensity is again \approx 2B, but the ridge point doubles too, to 3.94 \times 10^{14} / 8.2 \times 10^{11} = 480, so B > 240 — unchanged. What full int8 buys is wall-clock at a given batch, not a smaller batch.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What is the arithmetic intensity of [B, D] \times [B, D, F] \to [B, F] — a separate weight matrix per batch element — and what is the lesson?

html:div.html:details:
Answer In int8, the work is the same 2BDF — these are B independent [D] \times [D, F] products — but the traffic is BD + BDF + BF, dominated by the BDF weight term. So
\mathrm {Intensity} = \frac {2BDF}{BD + BDF + BF} \approx 2
constant. Batching bought nothing: B appears in numerator and denominator and cancels, leaving you comms-bound at every batch size.
The lesson is that a matmul's intensity comes entirely from amortizing one weight load across many tokens. Give every token its own weights and the amortization disappears — which is why per-example weights, and anything shaped like them, never reach the flat roof.

fr:title.text: The sharded-matmul threshold falls on D, not B

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The sharded-matmul threshold falls on D, not B

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Two chips split X[B, D] and Y[D, F] along D, each computing a partial sum and exchanging it. When is this compute-bound, and why is the threshold surprising?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Each chip does half the contraction, T_{\mathrm {math}} = BDF / 1.97 \times 10^{14}, then ships its [B, F] partial sum across the interconnect, T_{\mathrm {comms}} = 2BF / 4.5 \times 10^{10}. Compute-bound means
\frac {BDF}{2BF} = \frac {D}{2} > \frac {1.97 \times 10^{14}}{4.5 \times 10^{10}} = 4377 \implies D > 8755
The surprise is that the threshold depends on D, not B: the batch scales FLOPs and bytes-sent identically and cancels out. Same roofline machinery as a single-chip matmul, but because the relevant bandwidth is now the network, a different dimension decides whether Tensor Parallelism pays for itself — the contracted dimension has to be large enough to hide the exchange.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: VMEM vs HBM bandwidth: what is the ratio, and what does it do to the roofline?

html:div.html:details:
Answer VMEM\to MXU bandwidth is roughly 22\times HBM bandwidth, so the critical arithmetic intensity for peak FLOPs drops from ~240 to ~10–20.
Worked, with int8[16384,4096] weights on v5e: FLOPs-bound at B > 267 out of HBM, but only B > 11 out of VMEM — call it 20 in practice, since you cannot spend all of VMEM's bandwidth on weights.
The consequence is VMEM prefetch: load the FFW weights during attention and the load disappears behind compute. The limit is capacity — VMEM is tiny, so a layer's weights have to be small or sharded enough to fit with room to spare.

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Why the MXU pads everything to 128

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What is the native op of one Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU), and why does that force padding to 128?

html:div.html:details:
Answer One bf16[8,128] @ bf16[128,128] -> f32[8,128] every 8 cycles, on a 128 \times 128 systolic array — 256 \times 256 on v6e/Trillium.
The array's side length is fixed in hardware, so any matrix axis shorter than 128 (256 on v6e) is padded up to it, and the FLOPs spent on the padding are simply wasted. With 2–4 MXUs per core, tiling dimensions want to exceed 128 \times the MXU count.
Scale: roughly 5e13 bf16 FLOPs/s per MXU at 1.5 GHz, so about 2e14 per v5e chip. int8 runs ~2\times faster, int4 ~4\times .

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Sketch the dataflow through a 128 \times 128 systolic array (Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU)). Where does the pipeline bubble come from?

html:div.html:details:
Answer A 2D grid of 16,384 ALUs, each doing one multiply-add per cycle.
Weights (RHS, 128 \times 128) are pushed down from the top.
Activations (LHS, 8 \times 128) stream in from the left.
Each cell multiplies its overlapped pair, adds the partial sum arriving from above, and passes the result down.
The bubble: both operands are loaded diagonally, so the array needs a fill period before every cell is busy. Once filled, new LHS/RHS stream in back-to-back with no further bubble — which is why large matrices amortize the fill and small ones do not.

fr:title.text: The VPU is thirty times smaller than the MXU

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The VPU is thirty times smaller than the MXU

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Vector Processing Unit: what is its shape and throughput relative to the Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU), and which reductions are cheap?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Shape (8\ \text {sublanes}, 128\ \text {lanes}), with 4 independent ALUs per position and most ops at 1/cycle:
8 \times 128 \times 4 \times 1.75\mathrm {e}9 \approx 7\mathrm {e}12 \text { FLOPs/s}
on v5p — about 30\times less than the ~2e14 MXU FLOPs/s per core. VPU work is fp32.
Reductions along the sublane axis (the 8) are cheap: an intra-lane shuffle by 4/2/1 plus three pairwise adds. Cross-lane reductions need the separate XLU, which is slow and expensive.
Control is skewed the other way: a single scalar core fetches and dispatches everything and can issue only one DMA request per cycle. Efficient, but it blocks data-dependent vectorization.

fr:title.text: The three units and the one data path

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The three units and the one data path

fr:mainmatter.html:p: What are the three units inside a TPU TensorCore (TPU), and what is the data path from HBM to compute?

html:div.html:details:
Answer
MXU — matrix multiply on a systolic array. Nearly all of the FLOPs.
VPU — elementwise ops (ReLU, add, mul) and reductions.
VMEM — an on-chip scratchpad in the TensorCore, like L1/L2 but far larger (~128 MiB on v5e) and programmer-controlled rather than a cache.
The path is HBM \to VMEM \to VREGs \to MXU/VPU \to VMEM \to HBM. Nothing computes directly out of HBM. All of it is pipelined — the copies overlap with MXU work, so the array never stalls waiting on memory.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Name the four communication tiers on a TPU, fastest to slowest, with per-chip v5p numbers.

html:div.html:details:
Answer
HBM \leftrightarrow TensorCore — 2.8e12 B/s.
ICI (Inter-chip interconnect, chip to nearest neighbors) — 9e10 B/s per axis one-way, across 3 axes on v5p.
PCIe (host to its tray of chips) — 1.6e10 B/s, about 100\times slower than HBM.
DCN (host to host) — 6.25e9 B/s.
The design rule that falls out: keep the bytes crossing each channel proportional to that channel's speed. Note also that a TPU\to TPU transfer over DCN pays the whole chain — PCIe, NIC egress, NIC ingress, PCIe again.

fr:title.text: Which TPU axes actually wrap around

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Which TPU axes actually wrap around

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Inter-chip interconnect topology: which generations get which torus, and when do you actually get wraparound links?

html:div.html:details:
Answer
2D torus, 4 neighbors — v2, v3, v5e, v6e. A pod caps at 16 \times 16; past that, pods talk over DCN.
3D torus, 6 neighbors — v4, v5p. Superpods are 16 \times 16 \times 16 (v4) and 16 \times 20 \times 28 (v5p), built from reconfigurable 4 \times 4 \times 4 cubes joined by optical links.
Wraparounds exist only on full-cube multiples (4 \times 4 \times 4, 4 \times 4 \times 8 — not 2 \times 2 \times 4, since the optical switches only exist on a full cube), or on a v5e/v6e axis of exactly 16, so an 8 \times 16 slice wraps the long axis only. Losing the wraparound roughly doubles comms time.
Links are nearest-neighbor only and bypass the hosts entirely, so distant chips hop through the chips between them — unlike a GPU's switch hierarchy.

fr:title.text: Sharded Matrices and How to Multiply Them

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Sharded Matrices and How to Multiply Them

fr:title.text: An unsharded contracting axis needs no comms

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: An unsharded contracting axis needs no comms

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Sharded matmul, case 1: neither multiplicand has a sharded contracting dimension. What communication is required, and what is the output sharding?

html:div.html:details:
Answer None at all. Each device does a local block matmul and the result is already sharded correctly:
A[I_X, J] \cdot B[J, K_Y] \to C[I_X, K_Y]
The contracting axis J is unsharded, so every device holds complete contracting slices and the computation does not depend on the sharding. The output simply inherits the input shardings.
The one caveat: this holds only if the two inputs' non-contracting dimensions are not sharded over the same mesh axis — that case is invalid.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: An AllGather gets resources from all devices onto one device. In TPU's Ring topology, this is done in \frac {N}{2} hops via each TPU sending its shard to the neighboring chip.

Assuming we have X shards and the total bytes is N, then each chip must send \frac {N}{X} bytes. If we have an ICI bandwidth of W_{\text {ICI}}, then for each chip to send to its neighbor will be T_{1\text { hop}} = \frac {N}{X\cdot W_{\text {ICI}}} Now each chip must send across X hops, which gives T = X\cdot T_{1\text { hop}} = \frac {N}{W_{\text {ICI}}}.This does not change if we use the bi-directional bandwidth because then we have 2N bytes but only need to send at most \frac {X}{2} hops!
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. A super fun trick from [scaling-book, Ex 3.2]: If you have an unused replicated dimension, then you can shard the replicated axis and perform an AllGather over both dimensions to double your bandwidth!

fr:title.text: AllGather costs the same at any device count

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: AllGather costs the same at any device count

fr:mainmatter.html:p: AllGather: signature, mechanism, and cost?

html:span.style: font-family: var(--sans); font-size: 11pt; font-weight: 500; color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.65);

html:details.html:p: Signature [A_X, B] \to [A, B] — it removes a subscript, reassembling shards so every device on that axis holds a full copy. It can drop just one of several axes: A[I_{XY}, J] \to A[I_Y, J].
Mechanism: pass each shard around the ring, N-1 hops in one direction or about N/2 bidirectionally.

Cost, when bandwidth-bound: T = V / W_{\mathrm {ici}} on bidirectional bandwidth, or V / (W_{\mathrm {ici}} \cdot N_{\mathrm {axes}}) across several mesh axes. The takeaway is that this is independent of the device count X — each hop sends V/X bytes but you make X/2 hops. Only array size and link bandwidth matter.

Latency-bound regime: about 1\mu \mathrm {s} intrinsic cost per hop, so T = \max (T_{\min } \cdot \sum _i |X_i| / 2,\; V / (W \cdot N_{\mathrm {axes}})). On v5e (4.5e10 unidirectional) anything under ~45 kB is latency-bound.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Sharded matmul, case 2: one multiplicand has a sharded contracting dimension, A[I, J_X] \cdot B[J, K] \to C[I, K]. Which primitive, and what is the alternative?

html:div.html:details:
Answer AllGather the sharded input first, then matmul locally: \mathrm {AllGather}_X(A[I, J_X]) \to A[I, J], then A[I, J] \cdot B[J, K] \to C[I, K]. You cannot just multiply the local shards, because the sum over J is split across X and each device holds only a partial sum.
The alternative is to treat it like case 3: do the local partial matmul and AllReduce or ReduceScatter the result. That shards the FLOPs but usually costs more comms. For X[B,D] \cdot Y[D_X,F], the gather moves 2DF bytes and the reduce moves 2 \cdot 2BF, so the reduce path wins roughly when D > 2B.
Rare in practice, though — the other input is usually sharded along the same axis anyway, as under FSDP.

fr:title.text: A mesh axis may appear only once

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A mesh axis may appear only once

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Sharded matmul, case 4: both multiplicands have a non-contracting dimension sharded along the same mesh axis, A[I_X, J] \cdot B[J, K_X]. Why is this invalid, and how do you resolve it?

html:div.html:details:
Answer A mesh axis may appear at most once in a sharding. Writing C[I_X, K_X] would give shard i only the (i,i) block — the block diagonal. The off-diagonal blocks of C exist nowhere, so the result is unrecoverable.
The fix is to AllGather one of the two inputs along X first, so that X appears once in the output:
\mathrm {AllGather}_X(A) \to A[I, J], giving C[I, K_X].
\mathrm {AllGather}_X(B) \to B[J, K], giving C[I_X, K].
Which one you pick is decided by the sharding the downstream ops want.

fr:title.text: Matching contracting shards give partial sums

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Matching contracting shards give partial sums

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Sharded matmul, case 3: both multiplicands are sharded along the contracting dimension on the same mesh axis, A[I, J_X] \cdot B[J_X, K]. What happens, and which primitive fixes it?

html:div.html:details:
Answer The local shards can be multiplied — they share contracting indices — but each device ends up with only a partial sum, written C[I, K]\{U_X\}, "unreduced along X":
A \cdot B = \sum _i A[:,i] \otimes B[i,:]
Device i owns the i-th column block of A and the i-th row block of B, so it computes exactly the i-th term of that sum.
The fix is AllReduce along X for a replicated C[I, K] — or the cheaper \mathrm {ReduceScatter}_{X,K} \to C[I, K_X] if you can leave the output sharded. That is half the cost, and defers the gather, possibly forever.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The collective that resolves partial sums along a mesh axis and leaves the result sharded rather than replicated: [A, B]\{U_X\} \to [A_X, B]. It is the reduction half of an AllReduce, and the transpose of an AllGather. Same ring pass, same cost V / W_{\mathrm {ici}}, except each device sums the shard arriving from its left neighbour into its own copy instead of merely keeping it.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Notation. Because it introduces a subscript, you have to say where it goes: \mathrm {ReduceScatter}_{X,K} reduces along mesh axis X and shards the result along K. That freedom is the whole argument for preferring it. Namely, whenever the consumer can accept a sharded input, stopping at the ReduceScatter costs half what an AllReduce does and defers the gather, possibly forever.
fr:mainmatter.html:p: The mechanism is easiest to see as a schedule. Each device starts holding a full-size buffer that is only a partial sum, and on every step forwards one chunk rightward and folds in the chunk arriving from its left. After N-1 steps device b holds chunk b summed over all N partials and has forwarded the rest away, which is also why the resident memory falls by N.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Question. How do we know what chunk to send to who?

html:div.html:details: Answer.It is actually remarkably easy. If there are N devices, then you just compute which device is N - 1 hops away from you. You send that chunk to your right neighbor. Each chunk then propagates through the ring and will end up with the completed chunked sum on the correct device

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Note that the steps are not N-1 rounds of moving a whole buffer: every link carries one chunk in the same direction at the same time, so the cost is N-1 chunk-times, and the N in the chunk size cancels the N-1 in the step count. Nothing is ever broadcast, which is the sense in which the ring is optimal and the reason a ReduceScatter is not merely an AllReduce with a slice at the end.
ReduceScatter: signature, relationship to AllGather, and cost?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Signature [A, B]\{U_X\} \to [A_X, B] — it resolves partial sums along X and leaves the result sharded along a dimension of your choosing. It introduces a subscript, which is why you have to say where: \mathrm {ReduceScatter}_{X,K}.
Mechanism: the same ring pass as an AllGather, except you sum the incoming shards instead of keeping them. Cost is therefore identical, V / W_{\mathrm {ici}}.
Duality: AllGather and ReduceScatter are transposes of each other, hence each other's derivative — an AllGather in the forward pass means a ReduceScatter on the reverse-mode gradients, and vice versa. (Broadcast is u \otimes I, reduce is u^\top \otimes I.)

fr:title.text: AllReduce is two collectives, not one

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: AllReduce is two collectives, not one

fr:mainmatter.html:p: AllReduce: signature, decomposition, and cost relative to an AllGather?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Signature [A_X, B]\{U_Y\} \to [A_X, B] — it removes the "unreduced" suffix, leaving every device on the axis holding the same fully-summed value, unsharded along Y.
It is not really a primitive: an AllReduce is a ReduceScatter followed by an AllGather.
A[I_X, J]\{U_Y\} \xrightarrow {\ \mathrm {ReduceScatter}_{Y,J}\ } A[I_X, J_Y] \xrightarrow {\ \mathrm {AllGather}_Y\ } A[I_X, J]
Cost 2V / W_{\mathrm {ici}}, exactly 2\times an AllGather — which is the practical argument for stopping at the ReduceScatter whenever the consumer can accept a sharded output. The AllGather can then be deferred, or skipped entirely.

fr:title.text: AllToAll is a quarter of an AllGather

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: AllToAll is a quarter of an AllGather

fr:mainmatter.html:p: AllToAll: signature, when it shows up, and why is it cheaper than an AllGather?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Signature [A, B_X] \to [A_X, B] — a sharded transposition, which moves a subscript from one logical axis to another.
When: never out of a sharded matmul. It is for resharding between regions of a computation with incompatible layouts — classically MoE routing.
Cost V \cdot \max (A, B, C, \ldots ) / (4 N W_{\mathrm {ici}}); on a 1D mesh that is V / (4 W_{\mathrm {ici}}), a quarter of an AllGather, and it scales down further in 2D+ with the shortest axis.
Why cheaper, as 2 \times 2: each device need not send its whole shard everywhere, so the sum becomes D + (D-1) + \cdots + 1 instead of D repeated D times — a factor of 2. And bidirectionality buys 4\times here rather than the 2\times it buys an AllGather, since blocks travel at most D/2 hops in either direction. Equivalently: two random nodes on a ring are about N/4 hops apart.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The four collectives that sharded matmuls actually need, in the [scaling-book] notation: a subscript is a mesh axis the array is split along, and \{U_X\} marks an array that is unreduced along X — every device holds a full-size partial sum. A collective is then a rewrite of that decoration, and its cost is a function of how many bytes have to cross the ICI to do it.

html:tr.html:td: Gathers all the shards of a sharded array along an axis, removing a subscript.
Sums a partially summed array along an axis and shards it along another axis, adding a subscript.
Sums a partially summed array along an axis, removing the \{U_X\}. Combines an AllGather and a ReduceScatter.
Gathers (replicates) an axis and shards a different dimension along the same axis.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Only two of these are primitives. An AllReduce is a ReduceScatter followed by an AllGather, which is exactly why it costs twice as much, and the practical consequence is that you should stop at the ReduceScatter whenever the consumer can accept a sharded input. AllGather and ReduceScatter are transposes of each other and hence each other's derivative, so a forward-pass AllGather implies a ReduceScatter on the reverse-mode gradients.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. The runtime column is written relative to the AllGather because every entry is the same ring pass over the same V bytes — the only thing that changes is how far each byte travels. An AllToAll is 4\times cheaper because a shard's destination is on average a quarter of the ring away rather than all the way around, and no byte is broadcast to every device [scaling-book, Ex 3.10]. The \text {num\_axes} factor in the AllGather row is the trick from [scaling-book, Ex 3.2]: gathering over two mesh axes at once buys you both axes' bandwidth.

Remark. Notice what is absent from the runtime column: the number of devices. A ring collective moves V bytes off each chip regardless of how big the ring is, so cost depends on the array and the link, not the mesh size, which is what makes these affordable at pod scale and why the roofline question is comms-vs-FLOPs rather than comms-vs-devices.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A GPU sacrifices single-thread latency for aggregate throughput. The whole machine is built around the Thread-level parallelism design point — keep many threads resident, switch on every stall, spend almost no silicon on per-instruction control. The opposite end of the axis from a CPU:

The GPU equivalent of a core is a streaming multiprocessor (SM). Each SM executes the same instruction across many threads in lockstep — the SIMT programming model — and uses a per-register GPU register scoreboard rather than CPU-style wakeup-select to decide which warp can issue next.

Single instruction, multiple threads. A GPU streaming multiprocessor issues one instruction per cycle to a group of threads — a warp — but each thread within the group keeps its own program counter and register state. The hardware enforces lockstep execution within the warp while preserving the illusion of independent threads to the programmer.

SIMT is the GPU's answer to a question the Vector ISA / SIMD world struggled with: how do you get the throughput of wide vector execution without forcing the programmer to manually vectorize? Two mechanisms make this work.

fr:title.text: Warp divergence serializes both sides of a branch

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Warp divergence serializes both sides of a branch

fr:mainmatter.html:p: When threads in a warp take different branches of a conditional, the warp does not split into smaller warps. Instead, the active mask selects which lanes execute each branch; lanes on the inactive side run dummy instructions until the warp reconverges at the post-conditional join point. The programmer writes ordinary scalar code with if/else, and the hardware silently masks the inactive lanes.

This is the chief ergonomic win over SIMD: the compiler does not have to prove that all lanes will take the same path. The cost is that divergent code pays for both sides — a 32-wide warp where 16 threads take the if-branch and 16 take the else-branch executes both branches sequentially with half the lanes idle each time.

The hardware sequences the two paths with a reconvergence stack — or, on recent GPUs, a barrier-based equivalent that avoids its deadlocks. The standard software mitigation is Warp Specialization: group threads with the same control-flow trajectory into one warp so the branch never diverges in the first place.

Threads are assigned to warps based on warp-ID, but the hardware and compiler are free to regroup. Warp Specialization re-bundles threads with similar control-flow trajectories into the same warp so that future branches stay non-divergent. This is a class of optimization that pure SIMD cannot express — a SIMD ISA fixes the lane assignment at compile time.

The hardware cost of SIMT relative to SIMD is the per-thread PC and register state. The benefit is that a single binary runs efficiently across a wide range of dynamic control flow, which is why the model has dominated GPU programming since CUDA. The scoreboard mechanism described in GPU register scoreboard operates per-warp rather than per-thread precisely because SIMT treats the warp as the unit of issue.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. SIMT is sometimes described as "SIMD with a per-lane PC," which captures the implementation but understates the programming-model impact: vectorization becomes a runtime, not a compile-time, decision.

fr:title.text: Warp scheduling hides memory latency by switching among resident warps

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Warp scheduling hides memory latency by switching among resident warps

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A GPU keeps many warps resident on each Streaming Multiprocessor (SM) and switches between them on every stall. When a warp issues a memory op that misses cache it is dead for hundreds of cycles — but with dozens of resident warps the scheduler always has a runnable one, so aggregate throughput stays high even though single-warp latency is awful. This is the Thread-level parallelism design point cashed out on the GPU: spend silicon on resident warp state rather than on latency-reduction machinery. The switch is free because each SM's register file is large enough to hold every resident warp's registers at once, so a context switch is just changing which warp the scheduler picks — not saving state to memory the way a CPU context switch must.

Two things bound how well this works. Occupancy — how many warps are resident — sets the ceiling on latency hiding: with too few warps the scheduler runs out of runnable candidates. And the scheduler itself must stay cheap enough to choose a warp every cycle, which it does with a two-loop scoreboard check, marshalling each issued instruction's register reads through an operand collector.

The readiness-tracking structure that lets a GPU issue instructions out of program order without any of the CAM machinery a CPU needs. A scoreboard is a small table — typically one busy bit per architectural register — that records whether some in-flight instruction is still computing a value that something else might want to read.

The protocol is trivial. When an instruction issues, it sets the busy bit on its destination register. When it writes back, it clears the bit. Before any instruction can read its sources, the hardware checks the corresponding bits: if any source is busy, the instruction (or its entire warp) waits. The check is a single table lookup per source, so the per-instruction cost is O(1) regardless of how many other instructions are in flight.

This is enough because GPUs lean on Thread-level parallelism rather than Instruction-level parallelism. When a warp's next instruction reads a busy register, the GPU architecture scheduler does not stall — it picks a different ready warp from the dozens of resident warps and runs that one instead. The scoreboard's job is only to answer "is this warp ready? yes/no," which is far cheaper than the broadcast/compare a CPU Issue queue wakeup-select does to find dependency satisfaction in a single thread's instruction window.

The size difference falls out of this. CPU issue queues hold tens of entries; GPU instruction windows can hold many warps' worth of in-flight work, because every additional warp costs a row in the scoreboard and a register-file allocation, not a quadratic CAM expansion. See ILP vs TLP for why the design fork sits where it does.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. The scoreboard's simplicity is what lets GPUs spend their transistor budget on ALUs and the Register file instead of control logic. It is one of the most visible places where the Thread-level parallelism design choice cashes out as silicon savings.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A warp is the unit of scheduling on an NVIDIA GPU: a group of ~32 threads that issue one instruction per cycle in lockstep. Each functional unit in the SM has as many lanes as a warp has threads, so a single fetched instruction fans out across all 32 lanes at once. The warp — not the thread — is what the hardware fetches, schedules, and tracks; the per-thread SIMT programming model is an illusion built on top of it.

Because the warp is the atom of execution, the two facts that dominate GPU performance are both properties of the warp: it hides memory latency by switching among resident warps instead of stalling, and it serializes both sides of a branch when its threads diverge.
Grid: Top-level define how many blocks are needed to cover the computation across SMs.
Block: Ensures all warps in a block are resident on the same SM and have the same shared memory.
Warp: A group of 32 threads that execute the same instruction.
Thread: A single thread within a warp.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Shared memory on a GPU is a small (per-block) on-chip scratchpad with latency comparable to L1. Software-managed — the programmer explicitly stages data through it, the hardware does not cache for them. Used to:

html:ul.html:li: Avoid non-coalesced global accesses by reorganizing data layouts on the fly.
Reuse loaded data across threads within a block.
Communicate between threads within a block.

fr:title.text: Bank conflicts serialize shared-memory accesses to the same bank

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Bank conflicts serialize shared-memory accesses to the same bank

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Shared memory is divided into banks (typically 32). Each bank can service one access per cycle. If two threads in a warp access different addresses in the same bank, the accesses serialize — a bank conflict.
Three behaviors when warp threads access shared memory:

html:ul.html:li: Different banks: full parallelism. No conflict.
Same bank, same word: hardware broadcasts the word to all threads. No conflict.
Same bank, different words: serialize.

fr:mainmatter.html:div: Question. How to avoid bank conflicts?

html:div.html:details: Answer.Change the access pattern so threads hit different banks (often by transposing or by adding padding to break the stride that causes the conflict).

fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. The GPU memory hierarchy is software-managed at L1 (shared memory) and coherent only at L2 — by restricting L1 to local-to-block scope, the architecture sidesteps the cost of a global Cache coherence protocol on a thousand-way-parallel chip.

fr:title.text: Memory coalescing merges a warp's accesses into one transaction per cache line

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Memory coalescing merges a warp's accesses into one transaction per cache line

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The hardware optimization on GPUs that combines simultaneous memory accesses by threads in a warp into a single transaction — when the accessed addresses fall in the same cache line.
Global memory latency on a GPU is 400–800 cycles. Coalescing is the primary way to keep the SM fed:

html:ul.html:li: If all 32 threads in a warp access addresses within one cache line: one memory transaction, full bandwidth.
If addresses span multiple cache lines: the hardware serializes into multiple transactions; bandwidth drops proportionally.

fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. Address permutations within a cache line don't hurt utilization — coalescing is about which lines are touched, not which exact bytes.
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Coalescing is why memory layout matters so much for GPU code. The standard idiom is structure-of-arrays (SoA) instead of array-of-structures (AoS): threads accessing the same field of consecutive records hit consecutive bytes, which coalesce; threads accessing the same struct don't.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Question. Should you always cache on the GPU?

html:div.html:details: Answer.No. If you're memory-bound and have no Spatial locality, cache is wasted on data you won't reuse. CUDA exposes the option to disable L1 caching for these cases, which lets misaligned loads transfer only the bytes needed instead of full cache lines.

fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. Use GPUs for parallel parts where throughput dominates. Use CPUs for sequential parts where latency dominates — the ILP vs TLP axis is the right frame for deciding which.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A Graphics Processing Cluster (GPC) is a top-level hardware partition inside an NVIDIA GPU. It's one level up from the SM in the chip's hierarchy.
As of Hopper, SMs located in the same GPC are connected via an SM-to-SM network, enabling DSMEM.

A CTA is a group of threads that execute on the same Streaming Multiprocessor (SM), can synchronize via barriers (__syncthreads()), and share fast on-chip shared memory (Shared memory (GPU)). Threads within a CTA are scheduled and executed in groups of 32 called warps.

An sm_XX target is the compute capability a GPU kernel is compiled against — nvcc -arch=sm_90a — and it names an instruction surface, not a performance tier. fr:mainmatter.html:p: Read down the third column and the datacenter line tells one story: each generation moves the matrix multiply further away from the individual thread. mma.sync is issued by a warp and the operands live in its registers; wgmma is issued by a warpgroup of four and can read the A operand straight out of shared memory; tcgen05.mma is issued by a single thread on behalf of a CTA pair and keeps its accumulator in Tensor Memory (TMEM), a memory the register file does not see. The data movement follows the same arc — cp.async is a per-thread copy, Tensor Memory Accelerator (TMA) is a descriptor a single thread hands to a hardware engine.

The trap in the table is sm_120a. Consumer Blackwell shares the marketing generation with B200 but not the tensor-core path: it has Hopper-era conveniences (TMA, clusters, Distributed Shared Memory (GPU)) and Ampere-era MMA, with no tcgen05 and no TMEM at all. fr:mainmatter.html:p: The four collectives that sharded matmuls actually need, in the [scaling-book] notation: a subscript is a mesh axis the array is split along, and \{U_X\} marks an array that is unreduced along X — every device holds a full-size partial sum. A collective is then a rewrite of that decoration, and its cost is a function of how many bytes have to cross the ICI to do it.

html:tr.html:td: Gathers all the shards of a sharded array along an axis, removing a subscript.
Sums a partially summed array along an axis and shards it along another axis, adding a subscript.
Sums a partially summed array along an axis, removing the \{U_X\}. Combines an AllGather and a ReduceScatter.
Gathers (replicates) an axis and shards a different dimension along the same axis.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Only two of these are primitives. An AllReduce is a ReduceScatter followed by an AllGather, which is exactly why it costs twice as much, and the practical consequence is that you should stop at the ReduceScatter whenever the consumer can accept a sharded input. AllGather and ReduceScatter are transposes of each other and hence each other's derivative, so a forward-pass AllGather implies a ReduceScatter on the reverse-mode gradients.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. The runtime column is written relative to the AllGather because every entry is the same ring pass over the same V bytes — the only thing that changes is how far each byte travels. An AllToAll is 4\times cheaper because a shard's destination is on average a quarter of the ring away rather than all the way around, and no byte is broadcast to every device [scaling-book, Ex 3.10]. The \text {num\_axes} factor in the AllGather row is the trick from [scaling-book, Ex 3.2]: gathering over two mesh axes at once buys you both axes' bandwidth.

Remark. Notice what is absent from the runtime column: the number of devices. A ring collective moves V bytes off each chip regardless of how big the ring is, so cost depends on the array and the link, not the mesh size, which is what makes these affordable at pod scale and why the roofline question is comms-vs-FLOPs rather than comms-vs-devices.

Solution It is sharded across X, so that on each chip there is only 1/4 of A. However, it must be replicated across Y and Z which are 8\cdot 2 = 16 copies. This leaves us with 16 \times the total number of bytes across all copies.

How long should \text {AllGather}_{X}([B_X,D_Y]) take on a TPU v4p 4x4x4 slice with mesh Mesh({'X': 4, 'Y': 4, 'Z': 4}) if B=1024 and D=4096 in bfloat16? How about \text {AllGather}_{XY}([B_X,D_Y]) How about \text {AllReduce}_{Z}([B_X,D_Y]\{U_Z\})?
Solution
We cannot use bi-directional because we are on a non-16 dim axes on TPU v4p. Therefore, the ICI bandwidth is W_{\text {ICI}} = 4.5e10. From AllGather, we know that the communication time is independent of |X| and is \frac {N}{W_{\text {ICI}}}. For this problem, we have N = 1024\cdot 4096\cdot 2. Thus, it will take .186\text {ms}.
Remark. I do not understand wrap-around rules at allor maybe they are just highly unintuitive, but we actually do have bi-directional bandwidth. I also needed to take into consideration that |X| cancels out but we only have N/|Y| bytes. Correct answer is \frac {1024\cdot 4096\cdot 2}{9e10\cdot |Y|}
In this case, we now have double the bandwidth because we are reducing across both dimensions. However, the total number of bytes is now 4\times , which means this will be double the previous part.
An AllReduce requires each device to send the full A across Z. This should be \frac {2BD}{W_{\text {ICI}}} or 2 \times the previous part.
Remark. Completely misunderstood this question. For starters, when reducing along the Z axis, we still stay sharded across x and y and therefore do not make hops across those links. Therefore, we must divide by |X| \cdot |Y|. Also, I guess the heuristic that AllReduce is roughly 2 \times AllGather is used in calculations, which gives final answer \frac {4BD}{|X|\cdot |Y|\cdot W_{\text {ICI}}}

Let’s say we’re performing an \text {AllGather}_X([B_X]) but B is very small (say 128). How long should this take on a TPU v4p 4x4x4 slice with mesh Mesh({'X': 4, 'Y': 4, 'Z': 4}) in bfloat16?
Solution
Since |X| = 4, the hop latency time is \approx 4 \mu s. We have N = 2\cdot 128 = 256bytes and W_{\text {ICI}} = 9e10. This gives .0028 \mu s. So we are severely latency bound.
Remark. Only need to do 2 hops in bi-directional case, so true answer is \approx 2\mu s: still latency bound.

To perform X[B,D]\cdot _D Y[D_X,F] \to Z[B,F], in this section we tell you to perform \text {AllGather}_X(Y[D_X,F]) and multiply the fully replicated matrices (Case 2, Strategy 1). Instead, you could multiply the local shards like X[B,D_X]\cdot _D Y[D_X,F] \to Z[B,F]\{U_X\} (Case 3, Strategy 2), and then \text {AllReduce}_X(Z[B,F]\{U_X\}). How many FLOPs and comms does each of these perform? Which is better and why?
Solution
Case 2, strategy 1. In this case, the AllGather will take \frac {DF}{W_{\text {ICI}}} for communication over ICI and BD + DF + BF over HBM with 2BDF FLOPs.
Case 3, strategy 2. For local shards, each will only need to do \frac {2BDF}{X} FLOPs and BD + D_X F + BF HBM cost. However, the ICI cost would then be the whole matrix which is X \times as much over ICI.
Remark.
I was roughly correct. However, an important distinction (and gap in my understanding I gues) is that we have been ignoring HBM cost when communicating over ICI because these transfers are done concurrently and are therefore bottlenecked by the slower one (ICI).

Let’s say I want to do a matmul A[I,J]\cdot JB[J,K]\to C[I,K] on a TPU v4p 4x4x4 with the lowest possible latency. Assume the inputs can be sharded arbitrarily but the result should be fully replicated. How should my inputs be sharded? What is the total FLOPs and comms time?
Solution
My initial intuition is we do not want to shard along the contracting dimension. If we have a large enough matrix, then I think the best sharding strategy would be to shard A[I_{XYZ}, J], B[J, K]. The multiplication then requires no communication, and the only communication is an AllGather across all 3 axis, which should triple bandwidth. Since we shard over every axis of our mesh, we do not have any additional replicated bytes. This gives us N = 2IKbytes in bf16. Since we are on a 4\times 4\times 4 cube, we have bi-directional bandwidth availability. Therefore, the communication time on TPU v4p is \frac {2IK}{3\cdot 9e10}. The total flops is still just 2IJK.

A typical Transformer block has two matrices W_{in}[D,F] and W_{out}[F,D] where F \gg DF \gg D . Say we have a batch size B. Then the full block is In[B,D]\cdot W_{in}[D,F]\cdot W_{out}[F,D]. Let’s pick D=8192 , F=32768, and B=128 and assume everything is in bfloat16. Assume we’re running on a TPU v5e 2x2 slice but let’s pretend each TPU only has 300MB of free memory. How should In, W_{in}, W_{out}, and Out be sharded to stay below the memory limit while minimizing overall time? How much time is spent on comms and FLOPs? Hint: the final output doesn’t need to be fully replicated, but it should be sharded the same as the input so the “layer” can be repeated.
Solution
To start, lets compute how big everything is.
\begin {align*} In &= 2\cdot B\cdot D \\ &= 2\cdot 8192\cdot 128 = 2^{21} \\ W_{in} &= 2\cdot D\cdot F \\ &= 2\cdot 8192\cdot 32768 = 2^{29} \\ W_{out} &= 2\cdot D\cdot F \\ &= 2\cdot 8192\cdot 32768 = 2^{29} \end {align*}
and each TPU has 300MB \approx 300 \cdot 2^{20} \approx 2^{28} in this example. Therefore, each TPU can fit just over one half of W_{in} and W_{out}, which leads us to have to fully shard both across X and Y. The remaining 11 \cdot 2^{22} can fit \text {In}. However, we need to satisfy the constraint that \text {Out} is sharded in the same way as \text {In}. I propose first
Shard \text {In}[B_{XY}, D], W_{in}[D,F_{XY}]
Then, we are in case 1 and have an output of W_{mid}[B_{XY}, F_{XY}] with no communication necessary. However, we now need to multiply W_{mid} with W_{out}. I propose to
Shard W_{out}[F, D_{XY}]
This then requires two AllGather's. First, we have to AllGather W_{mid} along F. Then we perform the matmul between W_{mid} and W_{out}, which gives Out[B_{XY}, D_{XY}]. To provide \text {Out} as \text {In} to the next layer, we then must \text {AllGather}_{XY} along D.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: An AllGather gets resources from all devices onto one device. In TPU's Ring topology, this is done in \frac {N}{2} hops via each TPU sending its shard to the neighboring chip.

Assuming we have X shards and the total bytes is N, then each chip must send \frac {N}{X} bytes. If we have an ICI bandwidth of W_{\text {ICI}}, then for each chip to send to its neighbor will be T_{1\text { hop}} = \frac {N}{X\cdot W_{\text {ICI}}} Now each chip must send across X hops, which gives T = X\cdot T_{1\text { hop}} = \frac {N}{W_{\text {ICI}}}.This does not change if we use the bi-directional bandwidth because then we have 2N bytes but only need to send at most \frac {X}{2} hops!
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. A super fun trick from [scaling-book, Ex 3.2]: If you have an unused replicated dimension, then you can shard the replicated axis and perform an AllGather over both dimensions to double your bandwidth!

fr:title.text: AllGather costs the same at any device count

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: AllGather costs the same at any device count

fr:mainmatter.html:p: AllGather: signature, mechanism, and cost?

html:span.style: font-family: var(--sans); font-size: 11pt; font-weight: 500; color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.65);

html:details.html:p: Signature [A_X, B] \to [A, B] — it removes a subscript, reassembling shards so every device on that axis holds a full copy. It can drop just one of several axes: A[I_{XY}, J] \to A[I_Y, J].
Mechanism: pass each shard around the ring, N-1 hops in one direction or about N/2 bidirectionally.

Cost, when bandwidth-bound: T = V / W_{\mathrm {ici}} on bidirectional bandwidth, or V / (W_{\mathrm {ici}} \cdot N_{\mathrm {axes}}) across several mesh axes. The takeaway is that this is independent of the device count X — each hop sends V/X bytes but you make X/2 hops. Only array size and link bandwidth matter.

Latency-bound regime: about 1\mu \mathrm {s} intrinsic cost per hop, so T = \max (T_{\min } \cdot \sum _i |X_i| / 2,\; V / (W \cdot N_{\mathrm {axes}})). On v5e (4.5e10 unidirectional) anything under ~45 kB is latency-bound.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Sharded matmul, case 2: one multiplicand has a sharded contracting dimension, A[I, J_X] \cdot B[J, K] \to C[I, K]. Which primitive, and what is the alternative?

html:div.html:details:
Answer AllGather the sharded input first, then matmul locally: \mathrm {AllGather}_X(A[I, J_X]) \to A[I, J], then A[I, J] \cdot B[J, K] \to C[I, K]. You cannot just multiply the local shards, because the sum over J is split across X and each device holds only a partial sum.
The alternative is to treat it like case 3: do the local partial matmul and AllReduce or ReduceScatter the result. That shards the FLOPs but usually costs more comms. For X[B,D] \cdot Y[D_X,F], the gather moves 2DF bytes and the reduce moves 2 \cdot 2BF, so the reduce path wins roughly when D > 2B.
Rare in practice, though — the other input is usually sharded along the same axis anyway, as under FSDP.

fr:title.text: A mesh axis may appear only once

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: A mesh axis may appear only once

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Sharded matmul, case 4: both multiplicands have a non-contracting dimension sharded along the same mesh axis, A[I_X, J] \cdot B[J, K_X]. Why is this invalid, and how do you resolve it?

html:div.html:details:
Answer A mesh axis may appear at most once in a sharding. Writing C[I_X, K_X] would give shard i only the (i,i) block — the block diagonal. The off-diagonal blocks of C exist nowhere, so the result is unrecoverable.
The fix is to AllGather one of the two inputs along X first, so that X appears once in the output:
\mathrm {AllGather}_X(A) \to A[I, J], giving C[I, K_X].
\mathrm {AllGather}_X(B) \to B[J, K], giving C[I_X, K].
Which one you pick is decided by the sharding the downstream ops want.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The collective that resolves partial sums along a mesh axis and leaves the result sharded rather than replicated: [A, B]\{U_X\} \to [A_X, B]. It is the reduction half of an AllReduce, and the transpose of an AllGather. Same ring pass, same cost V / W_{\mathrm {ici}}, except each device sums the shard arriving from its left neighbour into its own copy instead of merely keeping it.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Notation. Because it introduces a subscript, you have to say where it goes: \mathrm {ReduceScatter}_{X,K} reduces along mesh axis X and shards the result along K. That freedom is the whole argument for preferring it. Namely, whenever the consumer can accept a sharded input, stopping at the ReduceScatter costs half what an AllReduce does and defers the gather, possibly forever.
fr:mainmatter.html:p: The mechanism is easiest to see as a schedule. Each device starts holding a full-size buffer that is only a partial sum, and on every step forwards one chunk rightward and folds in the chunk arriving from its left. After N-1 steps device b holds chunk b summed over all N partials and has forwarded the rest away, which is also why the resident memory falls by N.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Question. How do we know what chunk to send to who?

html:div.html:details: Answer.It is actually remarkably easy. If there are N devices, then you just compute which device is N - 1 hops away from you. You send that chunk to your right neighbor. Each chunk then propagates through the ring and will end up with the completed chunked sum on the correct device

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Note that the steps are not N-1 rounds of moving a whole buffer: every link carries one chunk in the same direction at the same time, so the cost is N-1 chunk-times, and the N in the chunk size cancels the N-1 in the step count. Nothing is ever broadcast, which is the sense in which the ring is optimal and the reason a ReduceScatter is not merely an AllReduce with a slice at the end.
ReduceScatter: signature, relationship to AllGather, and cost?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Signature [A, B]\{U_X\} \to [A_X, B] — it resolves partial sums along X and leaves the result sharded along a dimension of your choosing. It introduces a subscript, which is why you have to say where: \mathrm {ReduceScatter}_{X,K}.
Mechanism: the same ring pass as an AllGather, except you sum the incoming shards instead of keeping them. Cost is therefore identical, V / W_{\mathrm {ici}}.
Duality: AllGather and ReduceScatter are transposes of each other, hence each other's derivative — an AllGather in the forward pass means a ReduceScatter on the reverse-mode gradients, and vice versa. (Broadcast is u \otimes I, reduce is u^\top \otimes I.)

fr:title.text: AllReduce is two collectives, not one

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: AllReduce is two collectives, not one

fr:mainmatter.html:p: AllReduce: signature, decomposition, and cost relative to an AllGather?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Signature [A_X, B]\{U_Y\} \to [A_X, B] — it removes the "unreduced" suffix, leaving every device on the axis holding the same fully-summed value, unsharded along Y.
It is not really a primitive: an AllReduce is a ReduceScatter followed by an AllGather.
A[I_X, J]\{U_Y\} \xrightarrow {\ \mathrm {ReduceScatter}_{Y,J}\ } A[I_X, J_Y] \xrightarrow {\ \mathrm {AllGather}_Y\ } A[I_X, J]
Cost 2V / W_{\mathrm {ici}}, exactly 2\times an AllGather — which is the practical argument for stopping at the ReduceScatter whenever the consumer can accept a sharded output. The AllGather can then be deferred, or skipped entirely.

fr:title.text: Matching contracting shards give partial sums

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Matching contracting shards give partial sums

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Sharded matmul, case 3: both multiplicands are sharded along the contracting dimension on the same mesh axis, A[I, J_X] \cdot B[J_X, K]. What happens, and which primitive fixes it?

html:div.html:details:
Answer The local shards can be multiplied — they share contracting indices — but each device ends up with only a partial sum, written C[I, K]\{U_X\}, "unreduced along X":
A \cdot B = \sum _i A[:,i] \otimes B[i,:]
Device i owns the i-th column block of A and the i-th row block of B, so it computes exactly the i-th term of that sum.
The fix is AllReduce along X for a replicated C[I, K] — or the cheaper \mathrm {ReduceScatter}_{X,K} \to C[I, K_X] if you can leave the output sharded. That is half the cost, and defers the gather, possibly forever.

fr:title.text: The VPU is thirty times smaller than the MXU

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The VPU is thirty times smaller than the MXU

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Vector Processing Unit: what is its shape and throughput relative to the Matrix Multiply Unit (MXU), and which reductions are cheap?

html:div.html:details:
Answer Shape (8\ \text {sublanes}, 128\ \text {lanes}), with 4 independent ALUs per position and most ops at 1/cycle:
8 \times 128 \times 4 \times 1.75\mathrm {e}9 \approx 7\mathrm {e}12 \text { FLOPs/s}
on v5p — about 30\times less than the ~2e14 MXU FLOPs/s per core. VPU work is fp32.
Reductions along the sublane axis (the 8) are cheap: an intra-lane shuffle by 4/2/1 plus three pairwise adds. Cross-lane reductions need the separate XLU, which is slow and expensive.
Control is skewed the other way: a single scalar core fetches and dispatches everything and can issue only one DMA request per cycle. Efficient, but it blocks data-dependent vectorization.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The process abstraction, what the OS has to support to maintain it, and the data structure that holds it together.
A running program, plus all the state the OS needs to pause it and resume it later. A process consists of:

html:ol.html:li: Memory: an Address space holding the program's code, stack, and heap.
Registers: general-purpose registers carrying current computation, plus special-purpose registers:

html:ul.html:li: Program counter (PC): the next instruction to run.
Stack pointer and frame pointer: where the process sits on its stack.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A process moves between three states:

html:ul.html:li: running: currently on a CPU.
ready: runnable, waiting for the Scheduling to give it a CPU.
blocked: waiting on I/O or another event, not runnable.

fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. Threads (see Concurrency Intro) share an address space within a process but each have their own PC, register set, and stack.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The minimum operations any OS must expose for working with Processes:

html:ol.html:li: Create: load a program from disk, set up its address space (stack, heap, code), and jump to main. The OS also initializes argc/argv.
Destroy: kill a misbehaving or unwanted process.
Wait: block until another process completes — useful for ordering dependent work.
Miscellaneous control: e.g. suspend / resume.
Status: report on running processes.

fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. The stack is allocated up front. The heap starts small and grows via malloc, which calls into the OS (brk/sbrk) when it runs out of headroom.
fr:mainmatter.html:p: On Unix, the concrete realization of this API uses fork(), wait(), and exec() — covered separately.

The kernel-side data structure holding all per-process state. There is one PCB per Process, threaded together into the process list. The PCB is what the OS reads and writes during a Context switch: the saved register set lives here, as does the process state, the open files, the parent pointer, and so on.

Cycle through all runnable jobs, giving each a fixed time slice — the stride, time slice, or quantum length — before preempting and moving to the next. The best you can do at minimizing response time: every job sees the CPU within at most N quanta where N is the runnable-job count.
The quantum length is a tradeoff:

html:ul.html:li: Short quantum: better response time, more frequent context switches, worse cache locality.
Long quantum: amortizes context-switch cost, worse response time.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Worst-case response time for N jobs at quantum S is S(N-1).
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. Round-robin minimizes response time but is poor for turnaround time relative to STCF scheduling. A scheduler that wants both has to combine ideas — see Multi-level feedback queue.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Shortest job first. Run the job with the smallest total work first, run-to-completion. If all jobs arrive at the same time, SJF provably minimizes average turnaround time.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Problem. Real workloads don't all arrive at t = 0. A long job that arrives slightly before a short one still gets to monopolize the CPU until it finishes — SJF degenerates to FIFO scheduling under sequential arrivals.
fr:mainmatter.html:p: Removing the run-to-completion constraint and allowing preemption gives STCF scheduling.

First-in, first-out. Jobs are run to completion in the order they arrive. Trivially fair under any reasonable notion of fairness, but suffers from the convoy effect: a single long-running job at the head delays every shorter job behind it, inflating average turnaround time.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Problem. If the first arriving job is much longer than the rest, all subsequent jobs wait at least its full duration before getting any CPU.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: An asynchronous notification delivered to a Process. A process sends a signal with kill(pid, signum) (the name is misleading — most signals don't kill); the recipient can install a handler with signal(signum, handler) to "catch" it, otherwise the default action runs (often termination).

Signals are the OS's mechanism for events the recipient didn't ask to be told about: SIGINT from Ctrl-C, SIGSEGV from a Page fault on an invalid page, SIGCHLD when a child exits, SIGTERM from an administrative kill.
Who can signal whom depends on the user owning the process — a user can signal their own processes; the superuser can signal any process.

Replaces the calling Process's program with a new executable. exec() does not return on success — the original code, data, stack, and heap are discarded and the new program runs in their place. The PID is unchanged.
What exec() does internally:

html:ol.html:li: Loads the new executable's code and static data, overwriting the current.
Re-initializes stack and heap.
Jumps to the new program's entry point with arguments passed as argv.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The canonical Unix pattern is fork() then exec() — the shell uses this to launch a command without becoming that command:
Redirection is implemented by opening a file in the child between fork() and exec(), attached to STDOUT_FILENO:
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. The many variants — execl, execle, execlp, execv, execvp, execvP — differ in how they take arguments (list vs. vector), whether they use the PATH environment variable, and whether they take an explicit environment.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Blocks the calling Process until one of its children terminates. The OS marks the child's PCB ZOMBIE on exit, keeping enough state (exit status, resource usage) for the parent to retrieve via wait(); only when the parent collects it is the child fully reaped.
wait() returns the PID of the child that died. Variant waitpid(pid, ...) blocks on a specific child — useful when a parent has multiple children and only one is interesting.
Used to enforce ordering between parent and child code paths after fork(), or to know when an exec()'d program finishes.
fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. Calling wait() with no children to wait on returns -1.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The Unix system call that duplicates the calling Process. After fork() returns, two processes exist where there was one. The child gets its own copy of:

html:ol.html:li: Address space.
General-purpose registers.
Program counter — the child returns from fork() at the same instruction the parent does.

fr:mainmatter.html:div: Remark. Which process is scheduled first after fork() is non-deterministic. Use wait() if you need ordering.
Remark. The copy is logical, not physical: real implementations use Copy-on-write so the duplicated address space only allocates fresh pages when one side writes to them.
